During the Gilded Age, American railroad mileage tripled between 1860 and 1880, and tripled again by 1920, opening new areas to commercial farming, creating a truly national marketplace and inspiring a boom in coal mining and steel production. The voracious appetite for capital of the great trunk railroads facilitated the consolidation of the nation's financial market in [[Wall Street]]. By 1900, the process of economic concentration had extended into most branches of industry—a few large corporations, some organized as "trusts" (e.g. Standard Oil), dominated in steel, oil, sugar, meatpacking, and the manufacture of agriculture machinery. Other major components of this infrastructure were the new methods for manufacturing steel, especially the [[Bessemer process]]. The first billion-dollar corporation was [[United States Steel]], formed by financier [[J. P. Morgan]] in 1901, who purchased and consolidated steel firms built by [[Andrew Carnegie]] and others.<ref name="Edward C. Kirkland 1961">{{cite book |last=Kirkland |first=Edward C. |title=Industry Comes of Age, Business, Labor, and Public Policy 1860–1897 |year=1961}}</ref>

Increased mechanization of industry and improvements to worker efficiency increased the productivity of factories while undercutting the need for skilled labor. Mechanical innovations such as batch and continuous processing began to become much more prominent in factories. This mechanization made some factories an assemblage of unskilled laborers performing simple and repetitive tasks under the direction of skilled foremen and engineers. In some cases, the advancement of such mechanization substituted for low-skilled workers altogether. Both the number of unskilled and skilled workers increased, as their wage rates grew<ref>{{cite book |last=Calhoun |first=Daniel Hovey |title=The American Civil Engineer: Origins and Conflicts |year=1960}}</ref> Engineering colleges were established to feed the enormous demand for expertise. Together with rapid growth of small business, a new middle class was rapidly growing, especially in northern cities.<ref>{{cite book |last=Licht |first=Walter |title=Working for the Railroad: The Organization of Work in the Nineteenth Century |year=1983}}</ref>

==Germany==
The [[German Empire]] came to rival Britain as Europe's primary industrial nation during this period. Since Germany industrialized later, it was able to model its factories after those of Britain, thus making more efficient use of its capital and avoiding legacy methods in its leap to the envelope of technology. Germany invested more heavily than the British in research, especially in chemistry, motors and electricity. The German [[Concern (business)|concern]] system (known as ''Konzerne''), being significantly concentrated, was able to make more efficient use of capital. Germany was not weighed down with an expensive worldwide empire that needed defense. Following Germany's annexation of [[Alsace-Lorraine]] in 1871, it absorbed parts of what had been France's industrial base.<ref>Broadberry and O'Rourke (2010)</ref>

By 1900 the German chemical industry dominated the world market for [[Dye|synthetic dyes]]. The three major firms [[BASF]], [[Bayer]] and [[Hoechst AG|Hoechst]] produced several hundred different dyes, along with the five smaller firms. In 1913 these eight firms produced almost 90 percent of the world supply of dyestuffs, and sold about 80 percent of their production abroad. The three major firms had also integrated upstream into the production of essential raw materials and they began to expand into other areas of chemistry such as [[Drug|pharmaceuticals]], [[photographic film]], [[Agrochemical|agricultural chemicals]] and [[Electrochemistry|electrochemical]]. Top-level decision-making was in the hands of professional salaried managers, leading Chandler to call the German dye companies "the world's first truly managerial industrial enterprises".{{sfn|Chandler |1990| pp=474-475}} There were many spin offs from research—such as the pharmaceutical industry, which emerged from chemical research.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Burhop |first=Carsten |title=Pharmaceutical Research in Wilhelmine Germany: the Case of E. Merck |journal=Business History Review |volume=83 |issue=3 |year=2009 |pages=475+ |url=https://www.proquest.com}}</ref>

==Belgium==
[[History of Belgium|Belgium]] during the [[Belle Époque]] showed the value of the [[History of rail transport|railways]] for speeding the Second Industrial Revolution. After 1830, when it [[Belgian Revolution|broke away from the Netherlands]] and became a new nation, it decided to stimulate industry. It planned and funded a simple cruciform system that connected major cities, ports and mining areas, and linked to neighboring countries. Belgium thus became the railway center of the region. [[History of rail transport in Belgium|The system]] was soundly built along British lines, so that profits were low but the infrastructure necessary for rapid industrial growth was put in place.<ref>{{cite book |last=O'Brien |first=Patrick |title=Railways and the Economic Development of Western Europe, 1830–1914 |year=1983}}</ref>

== Poland (Russian Empire)==
In [[Central Europe|Central]] and [[Eastern Europe|Eastern]] Europe, the city of [[Łódź]] emerged as a premier industrial hub, earning the moniker ''The [[Polish people|Polish]] [[Manchester]]''<ref>{{Cite web |last=unlimited |first=communications |date=10 February 2017 |title=The city dubbed the Polish Manchester |url=https://www.communications-unlimited.nl/the-city-dubbed-the-polish-manchester/ |access-date=13 April 2026 |website=Communications Unlimited |language=en-GB}}</ref> or ''[[Ziemia obiecana|The Promised Land]]''. Following its [[Łódź#Partitions and development (1815–1918)|designation as a factory settlement in 1823]], the city underwent a demographic and industrial transformation that was unprecedented in the region. The arrival of the first steam engine in 1839 and the subsequent rail connection to the Warsaw-Vienna line in 1865 catalyzed its expansion. 

During the Second Industrial Revolution, Łódź became a global multicultural center for textile manufacturing, driven by massive integrated factory complexes such as those of [[Karl Wilhelm Scheibler|Karol Scheibler]] and [[Izrael Poznański]]. The city's growth was uniquely fueled by its role as a primary supplier to the vast markets of the [[Russian Empire]], leading to a population surge from under 1,000 inhabitants in 1823 to over 400,000 by the eve of [[World War I]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=History of Lodz – Industrial Revolution & Culture |url=https://www.kupi.com/en-ae/explore/poland/lodz/history |access-date=13 April 2026 |website=Kupi.com |language=en}}</ref>

==Alternative uses==
{{Original research|date=July 2024|reason=While there are Reliable sources that call earlier advances "industrial revolutions" there might not be any that then number following revolutions as the 2nd}}{{More citations needed|date=July 2024}}
There have been other times that have been called "second industrial revolution". Industrial revolutions may be renumbered by taking earlier developments, such as the rise of [[medieval technology]] in the 12th century,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gimpel |first=Jean |url= |title=The medieval machine: the industrial revolution of the Middle Ages |date=1977 |publisher=Penguin Books |isbn=978-0-14-004514-7 |location=New York}}</ref> or of ancient Chinese technology during the [[Tang dynasty]], or of [[ancient Roman technology]], as first. "Second industrial revolution" has been used in the popular press and by technologists or industrialists to refer to the changes following the spread of new technology after [[World War I]].

Excitement and debate over the dangers and benefits of the [[Atomic Age]] were more intense and lasting than those over the [[Space age]] but both were predicted to lead to another industrial revolution. At the start of the 21st century the term "second industrial revolution" has been used to describe the anticipated effects of hypothetical [[molecular nanotechnology]] systems upon society.<ref>{{Cite arXiv |last=Tahan |first=Charles |date=2006 |title=The Nanotechnology Revolution |eprint=physics/0612229 }}</ref> In this more recent scenario, they would render the majority of today's modern manufacturing processes obsolete, transforming all facets of the modern economy. Subsequent industrial revolutions include the [[Digital revolution]] and [[Environmental revolution]].
